candidates.title: Seven Riffles
candidates.pitch: A night-shift dealer swears three riffles is plenty. The visitor shuffles a drawn 52-card deck with a hand-made riffle (cut, then release), watches 'rising sequences' fan out like strands, and sees an exact meter of how far the deck still sits from truly random. Then they audit: run ten million seeded shuffles at 1 to 10 riffles and watch the chart show 'new deck order' and 'sorted suits' survive until the shuffle count nears seven.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless: the seven-shuffles slogan is half-known and widely misquoted, and it is a good argument to lose. Nothing similar has shipped.

research.summary: The Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model cuts a deck at a binomially distributed point and interleaves the two piles with probability proportional to pile sizes. Bayer and Diaconis showed the chance of any deck order after m riffles depends only on its number of rising sequences, so the distance from uniform for 52 cards can be computed EXACTLY (no sampling) and compared with Monte Carlo. Distance stays near 1 for about four to five riffles, then collapses (cutoff), and is under 0.5 at seven. The slogan depends on the metric: an entropy-based argument by other authors says five to six may do. That argument is the game: the visitor picks a yardstick and watches the verdict change. The uniqueness of every well-mixed deck (52 factorial is about 8.07e67) gives the closing line.

sources.title: Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model
sources.snippet: Defines the riffle model and reports that for 52 cards five riffles leave total variation distance near 1 while seven bring it to about 0.334.

sources.title: How many times should you shuffle the cards 2
sources.snippet: Computes total variation for 52 cards: close to 1 for the first four shuffles, below 0.5 at seven, below 0.1 by around nine; the sharp drop is called the cutoff.

sources.title: Factorial 52: A Stirling Problem
sources.snippet: Discusses the size of 52 factorial, about 8.07 times ten to the 67th, and how to approximate it.

sources.title: Each Shuffle of a Deck of Cards is Probably Unique in History
sources.snippet: Puzzle write-up giving 52 factorial as about 8.0658e67 and arguing a thoroughly shuffled order has almost certainly never occurred before, with caveats on shuffle quality.

sources.title: Riffle shuffle permutation
sources.snippet: Describes riffle permutations: one riffle gives the identity or exactly two rising sequences, so m riffles give at most 2 to the m.
sources.note: Rising-sequence structure (the build re-derives it by enumeration)

facts.claim: For a 52-card deck under the Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model, total variation distance from uniform is near 1 after five riffles and about 0.334 after seven (lecture notes: about 0.924 at five, 0.614 at six).
The distance stays close to 1 for the first four riffles, then drops sharply (cutoff); it is below 0.5 at seven riffles.
The number of orderings of a 52-card deck is 52 factorial, about 8.07e67.
Bayer and Diaconis relate the probability of a deck order after m riffles to its number of rising sequences, enabling exact computation instead of sampling.
Reported as of 2026-10-10 by Science News: an entropy-style argument says five to six riffles are enough, so the 'seven' slogan depends on the metric.

inspirations: the cutoff phenomenon in Markov chains
magician's faro and riffle control moves

design.coreLoop: Pick an opening deck (new-deck order, suits-grouped, a lightly pre-shuffled deck), riffle it yourself by dragging a cut and releasing, or press auto-riffle; read the rising-sequence strands and the live distance-from-random meter; try to find the smallest riffle count where a 'test' (e.g. how often the top card is an ace after a cut, or card-guessing score) stops betraying the original order. Daily challenge seeds give a shareable puzzle. It stays interesting because the meter, the exact formula and a Monte Carlo audit disagree in instructive ways until the visitor learns why.
sophisticationHooks: Exact total-variation distance for 52 cards via rising-sequence counts (Eulerian numbers), cross-checked by a seeded Monte Carlo of up to ten million riffles in a worker, with stated sample size and error bar
Yardstick switch: total variation, separation-style worst case, and an entropy-style meter, so the visitor sees the verdict move
A card-guessing duel: the page guesses each next card by exploiting residual order, scoring how well it beats chance after k riffles
Hand riffle by pointer drag with keyboard equivalent, and a URL hash carrying seed, deck, riffle count
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: GSR sampler, exact distance via Eulerian counts, canvas deck renderer with riffle animation (reduced-motion static fallback), worker Monte Carlo, guessing duel, hash state, about panel. Cut: other shuffle types (overhand, faro) beyond one comparison toggle, sound.
risks: The 0.334 and per-riffle distance figures vary slightly across sources; the page computes them itself and labels them as 'computed here', citing sources only for the slogan
Entropy-metric dispute (five to six riffles) rests on a single report; show as 'as of 2026-10-10, per Science News' or leave out
Exact computation for 52 cards needs big-number or log-space arithmetic; the cards specialist writes node self-checks against small n (n=3,4 brute force)
Scope: riffle animation art could eat the morning; mitigate with a simple two-pile slide animation

candidates.title: Second Pick Wins
candidates.pitch: Choose a three-flip coin pattern; a smug bot picks its own after seeing yours, and a flip-by-flip race decides who sees their pattern first. The visitor loses far more than half the time, for any pattern they try, then cranks the race to ten million flips and watches the bot's edge settle on exact fractions like 2 to 1, and finally flips the table by taking the second pick themselves. A red-and-black card mode with tricks turns the cascade of flips into a visible deck.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. The result is a clean argument-loser: the game is fair in each pick yet rigged by order of choice, and nothing like it has shipped.

research.summary: In Penney's game two players each pick a short heads-tails pattern and the one that appears first in a fair coin sequence wins. Because picking is sequential, the second picker can always choose a reply that beats the first pick; for every three-flip pattern a better reply exists. A short rule builds the reply, and Conway's leading-number method gives exact odds. A card version (red/black cards, collecting tricks) exists. The page can show the full payoff matrix of lengths 3 to 5, the exact Markov-chain odds next to a ten-million-flip seeded Monte Carlo, and expected waiting times, where the winning pattern is not always the quicker one on average, which is what makes the loss feel unfair.

facts.claim: In Penney's game the second chooser has an advantage: for any pattern of three flips there is another three-flip pattern strictly more likely to appear first.
Conway's leading-number algorithm gives the odds between two patterns; a no-arbitrage proof was published in 2019.
Reply rule: against a first pick, flip the second symbol, put it in front, and drop the last symbol; HTH is answered by HHT.
A card variant with red and black cards (Humble-Nishiyama) uses the same logic, with tricks collected instead of single wins.
Reported by one write-up: HHT precedes HTH about two thirds of the time; the page computes this exactly itself.

design.coreLoop: Pick a pattern (length 3, later 4 or 5); the bot answers; run one live race flip by flip with a bar-chart tension, then batches of 1,000 or 10 million; track the running win rate converging to the exact fraction. Modes: you pick first (you lose), the bot picks first (you find the reply and win), and a puzzle mode where you must find the pattern with the best guaranteed odds. Replay value comes from lengths 4 and 5, the card-deck mode where depletion changes the odds, and a streak of 'argument' challenges.
sophisticationHooks: Exact odds via Markov-chain absorption (Conway leading numbers cross-checked), versus seeded worker Monte Carlo with error bars
Payoff matrix heatmap for all patterns of length 3 to 5 with the best-reply path highlighted, plus a cycle view showing the non-transitive loop
Expected waiting time panel showing the pattern that arrives later on average still wins the race
Red/black deck mode played without replacement with tricks, so the visitor sees the effect survive in a real deck; hash state with seed and picks
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: pattern picker, bot reply engine, race animation, exact solver, worker Monte Carlo, payoff matrix, waiting-time panel, card mode, about panel, hash state. Cut: lengths above 5, multiplayer, sound.
risks: The 2 to 3 odds numbers beyond the sources are computed by the page and labelled 'computed here'
The ten-million-flip race must stay responsive: chunked in a worker with a progress bar
Card-mode odds differ from coin odds; both computed exactly by enumeration or DP and shown separately, never mixed
Plain Penney content is common online; the matrix, deck mode and waiting-time angle give it a distinct feel
